topics.title: Biot-Savart’s Law and Ampere’s Circuital Law

question.text: Consider a circular loop (radius $R$) carrying current $I$, the magnetic field produced by it at a point on the axis at a distance $z$ from the centre of the loop is $\dfrac{xR^2}{(z^2 + R^2)^{3/2}}$. The value of $x$ is

solution.text:
The magnetic field at a point on the axis of a circular loop of radius $R$ carrying current $I$, at a distance $z$ from its centre is given by Biot-Savart's law as:

$B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I R^2}{2(z^2 + R^2)^{3/2}}$

Comparing this with the given expression $B = \dfrac{xR^2}{(z^2 + R^2)^{3/2}}$, we get:

$x = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2}$

Answer: $\dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2}$

question.text: A particle carrying a charge equal to $100$ times the charge of an electron is rotating one rotation per second in a circular path of radius $0.8$ m. The value of magnetic field produced at the centre will be ($\mu_0$ = permeability of free space)

solution.text:
Charge of the particle, $q = 100e = 100 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} = 1.6 \times 10^{-17}$ C.

Frequency of rotation, $f = 1$ rev/s.

Equivalent current, $I = qf = 1.6 \times 10^{-17} \times 1 = 1.6 \times 10^{-17}$ A.

Magnetic field at the centre of the circular path is given by $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2r}$.

Substituting the values:

$B = \dfrac{\mu_0 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-17}}{2 \times 0.8}$

$B = \dfrac{\mu_0 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-17}}{1.6} = \mu_0 10^{-17}$ T.

Answer: $\mu_0 10^{-17}$

question.text: The magnitude of magnetic induction at a point on the axis at a large distance $r$ from a centre of a circular coil of $n$ turns and area $A$ carrying current $i$ is ($\mu_0$ = permeability of free space)

solution.text:
The magnetic field on the axis of a circular coil of $n$ turns and radius $R$ at a distance $r$ from its centre is given by

$B = \dfrac{\mu_0 n i R^2}{2(R^2 + r^2)^{3/2}}$

For a large distance $r \gg R$, the expression simplifies to

$B \approx \dfrac{\mu_0 n i R^2}{2 r^3}$

The area of the circular coil is $A = \pi R^2$, which gives $R^2 = \dfrac{A}{\pi}$. Substituting this into the equation for $B$, we get

$B = \dfrac{\mu_0 n i \left(\dfrac{A}{\pi}\right)}{2 r^3} = \dfrac{\mu_0 n i A}{2 \pi r^3}$

Multiplying the numerator and denominator by $2$, we obtain

$B = \dfrac{2\mu_0 n i A}{4\pi r^3}$

Alternatively, the coil acts as a magnetic dipole with magnetic moment $M = n i A$. The magnetic field on the axis of a dipole at a large distance $r$ is

$B = \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi} \dfrac{2M}{r^3} = \dfrac{2\mu_0 n i A}{4\pi r^3}$

Answer: $\dfrac{2\mu_0 niA}{4\pi r^3}$

question.text: Six very long insulated copper wires are bound together to form a cable. The currents carried by the wires are $i_1 = 10$A, $i_2 = -13$A, $i_3 = 10$A, $i_4 = 7$A, $i_5 = -12$A and $i_6 = 18$ A. The magnetic induction at a perpendicular distance of $10$ cm from the cable is $(\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}$ SI units$)$

solution.text:
The net current in the cable is the algebraic sum of the currents in the individual wires.

$I = i_1 + i_2 + i_3 + i_4 + i_5 + i_6$

$I = 10 - 13 + 10 + 7 - 12 + 18 = 20$ A

The magnetic induction $B$ at a perpendicular distance $r$ from a long straight cable carrying current $I$ is given by Ampere's Law:

$B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}$

Given $r = 10$ cm $= 0.1$ m and $\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}$ T m/A, substituting the values:

$B = \dfrac{4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times 20}{2\pi \times 0.1}$

$B = \dfrac{2 \times 10^{-7} \times 20}{0.1}$

$B = 400 \times 10^{-7}$ T

$B = 40 \times 10^{-6}$ T $= 40$ $\mu$T

Answer: $40$ $\mu$T

question.text: A current carrying circular coil of radius 'R' produces magnetic field $B_1$ at an axial point P at a distance 'x' from its centre and $B_2$ at point Q placed at its centre respectively . If $B_2 = 8B_1$, the value of x is

solution.text:
Magnetic field at an axial point P at a distance $x$ from the centre of a circular coil of radius $R$ is given by:

$B_1 = \dfrac{\mu_0 I R^2}{2(R^2 + x^2)^{3/2}}$

Magnetic field at the centre Q of the coil is given by:

$B_2 = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2R}$

Given that $B_2 = 8B_1$, substituting the expressions for $B_1$ and $B_2$:

$\dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2R} = 8 \left( \dfrac{\mu_0 I R^2}{2(R^2 + x^2)^{3/2}} \right)$

$\dfrac{1}{R} = \dfrac{8R^2}{(R^2 + x^2)^{3/2}}$

$(R^2 + x^2)^{3/2} = 8R^3$

Taking the cube root on both sides:

$(R^2 + x^2)^{1/2} = 2R$

Squaring both sides:

$R^2 + x^2 = 4R^2$

$x^2 = 3R^2$

$x = \sqrt{3}R$

Answer: $\sqrt{3}\,R$

question.text: Two circular coils X (smaller) and Y (bigger), each having a single turn, carry equal currents in the same direction and subtend the same angle at point 'O' along the axis of the coil. The distances of the centers of coil to point 'O' are $d$ and $\left(\dfrac{d}{2}\right)$ for coil Y and X respectively. The radii of coils Y and X are $(2r)$ and $(r)$ respectively. The magnetic induction due to the bigger coil at point 'O' is $B_y$ and that due to smaller coil X at point 'O' is $B_x$. ($d \gg r$) The relation between $B_x$ and $B_y$ is

solution.text:
The magnetic field on the axis of a circular coil of radius $R$ at a distance $x$ from its center is given by:

$B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I R^2}{2(R^2 + x^2)^{3/2}}$

For coil Y (bigger coil):
Radius $R_y = 2r$, distance $x_y = d$.

$B_y = \dfrac{\mu_0 I (2r)^2}{2((2r)^2 + d^2)^{3/2}} = \dfrac{4\mu_0 I r^2}{2(4r^2 + d^2)^{3/2}} = \dfrac{2\mu_0 I r^2}{(4r^2 + d^2)^{3/2}}$

For coil X (smaller coil):
Radius $R_x = r$, distance $x_x = \dfrac{d}{2}$.

$B_x = \dfrac{\mu_0 I r^2}{2\left(r^2 + \left(\dfrac{d}{2}\right)^2\right)^{3/2}} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I r^2}{2\left(\dfrac{4r^2 + d^2}{4}\right)^{3/2}} = \dfrac{8\mu_0 I r^2}{2(4r^2 + d^2)^{3/2}} = \dfrac{4\mu_0 I r^2}{(4r^2 + d^2)^{3/2}}$

Comparing the expressions for $B_x$ and $B_y$, we get:

$B_x = 2B_y$

Answer: $B_x = 2B_y$

question.text: Two wires with current 3A and 1.5A are enclosed in a circular loop P. Third parallel wire with current 1A is situated outside the loop as shown. All the wires are perpendicular to the plane of the circular loop. The value of $\oint \vec{B} \cdot \vec{dl}$ around the loop is ($\mu_0 = $ permeability of free space)

solution.text:
According to Ampere's circuital law, the line integral of the magnetic field $\vec{B}$ around any closed loop is equal to $\mu_0$ times the net current enclosed by the loop:

$\oint \vec{B} \cdot d\vec{l} = \mu_0 I_{\text{enclosed}}$

From the given figure, the loop P encloses two wires carrying currents $3\text{ A}$ (upwards) and $1.5\text{ A}$ (downwards). The third wire carrying $1\text{ A}$ is outside the loop and does not contribute to the enclosed current.

Taking the upward direction as positive, the net enclosed current is:

$I_{\text{enclosed}} = 3 - 1.5 = 1.5\text{ A}$

Therefore, the value of the integral is:

$\oint \vec{B} \cdot d\vec{l} = \mu_0 (1.5) = 1.5\mu_0$

Answer: $1.5\,\mu_0$

question.text: The magnetic field at a distance 'r' from a long straight wire carrying current I is 0.4 tesla. The magnetic field at a distance 2r will be

solution.text:
The magnetic field due to a long straight wire carrying current $I$ at a distance $r$ is given by $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2 \pi r}$.

This implies that $B \propto \dfrac{1}{r}$.

Let the magnetic field at distance $r$ be $B_1 = 0.4$ T.

At distance $2r$, the magnetic field $B_2$ will be:

$\dfrac{B_2}{B_1} = \dfrac{r}{2r} = \dfrac{1}{2}$

$B_2 = \dfrac{B_1}{2} = \dfrac{0.4}{2} = 0.2$ T.

Answer: $0 \cdot 2$ tesla

question.text: The magnitude of magnetic induction at mid point 'O' due to current arrangement as shown in figure will be ($\mu_0$ = permeability of free space)

solution.text:
From the given figure, the horizontal distance between the vertical wire segment BC and the vertical wire segment ET is $a$.

Since point O is the midpoint, the perpendicular distance from O to each of these vertical segments is $a/2$.

Assuming the horizontal wire segments AB and DE are collinear and their extended axis passes through O, the magnetic field produced by them at point O is zero.

The vertical segment BC acts as a semi-infinite straight wire with its end at the level of O. The magnetic induction at O due to BC is $B_1 = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi(a/2)} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi a}$. By the right-hand thumb rule, its direction is perpendicular to the plane of the paper, pointing outwards.

The vertical segment ET also acts as a semi-infinite straight wire with its end at the level of O. The magnetic induction at O due to ET is $B_2 = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi(a/2)} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi a}$. By the right-hand thumb rule, its direction is also perpendicular to the plane of the paper, pointing outwards.

Since both magnetic fields are in the same direction, the total magnetic induction at O is the sum of their magnitudes:

$B = B_1 + B_2$

$B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi a} + \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi a} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{\pi a}$

question.text: A circular loop of radius R is carrying current I. The ratio of magnetic field at the center of circular loop and at a distance R from the center of the loop on its axis is

solution.text:
The magnetic field at the center of a circular loop of radius $R$ carrying current $I$ is given by:

$B_{center} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2R}$

The magnetic field on the axis of the circular loop at a distance $x$ from the center is given by:

$B_{axis} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I R^2}{2(R^2 + x^2)^{3/2}}$

Substituting $x = R$, we get:

$B_{axis} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I R^2}{2(R^2 + R^2)^{3/2}} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I R^2}{2(2R^2)^{3/2}} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I R^2}{2(2\sqrt{2}R^3)} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4\sqrt{2}R}$

The ratio of the magnetic fields is:

$\dfrac{B_{center}}{B_{axis}} = \dfrac{\dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2R}}{\dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4\sqrt{2}R}} = \dfrac{4\sqrt{2}}{2} = 2\sqrt{2} = \sqrt{8}$

The required ratio is $\sqrt{8} : 1$.

question.text: A current ' i ' is flowing in a conductor PQRST as shown in figure. The radius of curved path QRS is ' r ' and length of straight portion PQ and ST is very large. The magnetic field at the centre [O] of the curved part is ($\mu_0=$ permeability of free space)

solution.text:
The conductor can be divided into three parts: the semi-infinite straight wire PQ, the circular arc QRS, and the semi-infinite straight wire ST.

1. Magnetic field due to the straight wire PQ at O:
The extended line of the wire PQ passes through the center O. Therefore, the angle between the current element $d\vec{l}$ and the position vector $\vec{r}$ is zero. Thus, the magnetic field produced by this segment at O is zero.
$\vec{B}_{PQ} = 0$

2. Magnetic field due to the circular arc QRS at O:
The arc QRS subtends an angle of $360^\circ - 90^\circ = 270^\circ = \dfrac{3\pi}{2}$ radians at the center O. The current flows in a counterclockwise direction. According to the right-hand thumb rule, the magnetic field at O is directed outwards, i.e., in the $+\hat{k}$ direction.
$\vec{B}_{QRS} = \dfrac{\mu_0 i}{4\pi r} \theta \, \hat{k} = \dfrac{\mu_0 i}{4\pi r} \left(\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\right) \hat{k}$

3. Magnetic field due to the semi-infinite straight wire ST at O:
The wire ST is a semi-infinite straight wire starting from S and extending to infinity. The perpendicular distance from O to the wire is $r$. The point O lies exactly above the starting point S of the wire. The angles subtended by the ends of the wire at O are $\theta_1 = 90^\circ$ (for the end at infinity) and $\theta_2 = 0^\circ$ (for the end at S). The current flows to the right, so by the right-hand thumb rule, the magnetic field at O is directed outwards ($+\hat{k}$).
$\vec{B}_{ST} = \dfrac{\mu_0 i}{4\pi r} (\sin 90^\circ + \sin 0^\circ) \, \hat{k} = \dfrac{\mu_0 i}{4\pi r} (1 + 0) \, \hat{k} = \dfrac{\mu_0 i}{4\pi r} \hat{k}$

Total magnetic field at O is the vector sum of the magnetic fields due to all three parts:
$\vec{B}_{net} = \vec{B}_{PQ} + \vec{B}_{QRS} + \vec{B}_{ST}$

$\vec{B}_{net} = 0 + \dfrac{\mu_0 i}{4\pi r} \left(\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\right) \hat{k} + \dfrac{\mu_0 i}{4\pi r} \hat{k}$

$\vec{B}_{net} = \dfrac{\mu_0 i}{4\pi r} \left(\dfrac{3\pi}{2} + 1\right) \hat{k}$

Answer: $\frac{\mu_0 \mathrm{i}}{4 \pi \mathrm{r}}\left(\frac{3 \pi}{2}+1\right) \widehat{\mathrm{k}}$

question.text: An element $\overrightarrow{\Delta \ell}=\Delta \mathrm{x} \hat{\mathrm{i}}$ is placed at the origin and carries a current of 10A. The magnitude of magnetic field on the Y axis at a distance of 0.5 m if $\Delta \mathrm{x}=1 \mathrm{~cm}$ is $\left(\frac{\mu_0}{4 \pi}=10^{-7}\right.$ SI unit $)\left(\sin 90^{\circ}=1\right)$

solution.text:
According to Biot-Savart law, the magnitude of the magnetic field due to a current element is given by:

$dB = \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi} \dfrac{I dl \sin\theta}{r^2}$

Given:
$I = 10$ A
$dl = \Delta x = 1$ cm $= 10^{-2}$ m
$r = 0.5$ m
$\dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi} = 10^{-7}$ T m/A

Since the current element is along the X-axis and the point is on the Y-axis, the angle between them is $\theta = 90^\circ$.

Substituting the values into the formula:

$dB = 10^{-7} \times \dfrac{10 \times 10^{-2} \times \sin 90^\circ}{(0.5)^2}$

$dB = 10^{-7} \times \dfrac{10^{-1}}{0.25}$

$dB = \dfrac{10^{-8}}{0.25}$

$dB = 4 \times 10^{-8}$ T

Answer: $4 \times 10^{-8} \mathrm{~T}$

question.text: Two wires carrying current $5 \mathrm{~A}$ and $2 \mathrm{~A}$ are enclosed in a circular loop as shown in the figure. Another wire carrying a current of $3 \mathrm{~A}$ is situated outside the loop. The value of $f \overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}} \overrightarrow{\mathrm{dl}}$ around the loop is ( $\mu_0=$ permeability of free space, $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{dl}}$ is the length of the Amperion loop)

solution.text: Current of 5A and 2A are enclosed in the loop and are in opposite direction. Hence, net current enclosed by the loop is $3 \mathrm{~A}$. According to Ampere law, $\int \overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}} \cdot \overrightarrow{\mathrm{d} \mathrm{l}}=\mu_0 \sum \mathrm{I}=3 \mu_0$

question.text: A straight wire carrying current 'I' is bent into a semi-circular arc of radius ${ }^{\prime} \mathrm{r}^{\prime}$, as shown. The magnitude of magnetic field at point '0' due to semi-circular arc is $\left(\mu_{0}=\right.$ Permeability of free space)

A circular coil having n turns, each of radius 'r' carries a current I. The magnetic field at a distance $x = \sqrt{8}\, r$ from its centre along the axis of the coil is ($\mu_0$ = permeability of free space)

solution.text:
The magnetic field at a distance $x$ from the centre of a circular coil of $n$ turns and radius $r$ along its axis is given by

$B = \dfrac{\mu_0 n I r^2}{2(r^2 + x^2)^{3/2}}$

Given $x = \sqrt{8} r$, substituting this value in the formula gives

$B = \dfrac{\mu_0 n I r^2}{2(r^2 + (\sqrt{8} r)^2)^{3/2}}$

$B = \dfrac{\mu_0 n I r^2}{2(r^2 + 8r^2)^{3/2}}$

$B = \dfrac{\mu_0 n I r^2}{2(9r^2)^{3/2}}$

$B = \dfrac{\mu_0 n I r^2}{2(27r^3)}$

$B = \dfrac{\mu_0 n I}{54r}$

Answer: $\dfrac{\mu_0 nI}{54r}$

question.text: The magnitude of the magnetic field inside a long solenoid is increased by

options.label: D
options.text: introducing a medium of higher permeability

solution.text:
The magnetic field inside a long solenoid is given by $B = \mu n I$

where $\mu$ is the permeability of the medium inside the solenoid, $n$ is the number of turns per unit length, and $I$ is the current.

From the formula, the magnetic field $B$ is directly proportional to the permeability $\mu$ of the medium. Therefore, introducing a medium of higher permeability will increase the magnitude of the magnetic field.

The magnetic field of an ideal long solenoid is independent of its radius or area of cross-section, and decreasing the current would decrease the magnetic field.

Answer: introducing a medium of higher permeability

question.text: Two circular coils A and B are made from same wire but the radius of coil A is twice that of coil B. If the magnetic field at their centres is same then the ratio potential difference applied across them is

solution.text:
The magnetic field at the centre of a circular coil of $N$ turns and radius $R$ is given by:

$B = \dfrac{\mu_0 N I}{2 R}$

From this, the current $I$ in the coil is:

$I = \dfrac{2 R B}{\mu_0 N}$

The resistance of the coil is given by $R' = \rho \dfrac{l}{a}$, where $l$ is the total length of the wire and $a$ is its cross-sectional area. Since the coil has $N$ turns of radius $R$, the length is $l = N(2\pi R)$.

$R' = \rho \dfrac{N(2\pi R)}{a}$

The potential difference $V$ applied across the coil is:

$V = I R' = \left(\dfrac{2 R B}{\mu_0 N}\right) \left(\rho \dfrac{N(2\pi R)}{a}\right)$

$V = \dfrac{4 \pi \rho B R^2}{\mu_0 a}$

Since both coils are made from the same wire, $\rho$ and $a$ are constant. We are also given that the magnetic field $B$ at their centres is the same. Therefore, the potential difference is directly proportional to the square of the radius:

$V \propto R^2$

Given that the radius of coil A is twice that of coil B ($R_A = 2R_B$):

$\dfrac{V_A}{V_B} = \left(\dfrac{R_A}{R_B}\right)^2 = (2)^2 = 4$

The ratio of the potential difference applied across them is $4:1$.

Answer: $4:1$

question.text: Two parallel long wires carry currents $i_1$ and $i_2$ with $i_1 > i_2$. When the currents are in the same direction, the magnetic field at a point midway between the wires is $10\ \mu$T. If the direction of $i_2$ is reversed then the field becomes $30\ \mu$T. The ratio $\dfrac{i_1}{i_2}$

solution.text:
Let the distance between the two parallel wires be $2d$. The magnetic field at the midpoint due to a long straight wire carrying current $i$ is given by $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 i}{2\pi d}$.

When the currents are in the same direction, the magnetic fields produced by the two wires at the midpoint are in opposite directions. Since $i_1 > i_2$, the net magnetic field is:

$B_1 = \dfrac{\mu_0}{2\pi d}(i_1 - i_2) = 10\ \mu\text{T}$

When the direction of $i_2$ is reversed, the currents are in opposite directions, and their magnetic fields at the midpoint add up. The net magnetic field becomes:

$B_2 = \dfrac{\mu_0}{2\pi d}(i_1 + i_2) = 30\ \mu\text{T}$

Dividing the second equation by the first equation, we get:

$\dfrac{i_1 + i_2}{i_1 - i_2} = \dfrac{30}{10} = 3$

$i_1 + i_2 = 3i_1 - 3i_2$

$2i_1 = 4i_2$

$\dfrac{i_1}{i_2} = 2$

Answer: $2$

question.text: Two circular coils $A$ and $B$ are made from the same wire but the radius of coil $A$ is twice that of coil $B$. What is the ratio of potential difference applied across them, so that the magnetic field at their centres is the same?

solution.text:
Let the resistance per unit length of the wire be $\lambda$.

For a circular coil of radius $R$ having a single turn, the length of the wire is $2\pi R$.

The resistance of the coil is given by:
$R_c = \lambda (2\pi R)$

The magnetic field at the centre of a circular coil carrying current $I$ is:
$B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2R}$

Using Ohm's law, the current $I$ can be written in terms of the applied potential difference $V$ as:
$I = \dfrac{V}{R_c} = \dfrac{V}{\lambda (2\pi R)}$

Substituting this into the magnetic field formula, we get:
$B = \dfrac{\mu_0}{2R} \left( \dfrac{V}{\lambda 2\pi R} \right) = \dfrac{\mu_0 V}{4\pi \lambda R^2}$

We are given that the magnetic field at the centre of both coils is the same ($B_A = B_B$):
$\dfrac{\mu_0 V_A}{4\pi \lambda R_A^2} = \dfrac{\mu_0 V_B}{4\pi \lambda R_B^2}$

$\Rightarrow \dfrac{V_A}{V_B} = \left( \dfrac{R_A}{R_B} \right)^2$

Given that the radius of coil $A$ is twice that of coil $B$ ($R_A = 2R_B$), we have $\dfrac{R_A}{R_B} = 2$.

$\Rightarrow \dfrac{V_A}{V_B} = (2)^2 = 4$

Therefore, the ratio of the potential difference applied across them is $4 : 1$.

Answer: $4 : 1$

question.text: The magnitude of the magnetic field inside a long solenoid is increased by

options.label: D
options.text: introducing a medium of higher permeability

solution.text:
The magnitude of the magnetic field inside a long solenoid is given by the formula $B = \mu n I$, where $\mu$ is the permeability of the medium inside the solenoid, $n$ is the number of turns per unit length, and $I$ is the current flowing through it.

From the formula, the magnetic field is directly proportional to the permeability of the medium ($B \propto \mu$) and the current ($B \propto I$). It is independent of the radius or the area of cross-section of the solenoid.

Therefore, introducing a medium of higher permeability will increase the magnitude of the magnetic field inside the solenoid.

Answer: introducing a medium of higher permeability

question.text: An arc of a circle of radius R subtends an angle $\pi/2$ at the centre. It carries a current I. The magnetic field at the centre will be ($\mu_0$ = permeability of free space)

solution.text:
The magnetic field at the centre of a circular arc subtending an angle $\theta$ at the centre is given by

$B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi R} \theta$

Given that the arc subtends an angle $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$ at the centre.

Substituting the value of $\theta$ in the formula, we get

$B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi R} \times \dfrac{\pi}{2}$

$B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{8R}$

Answer: $\dfrac{\mu_0 I}{8R}$

question.text: Two parallel wires of equal lengths are separated by a distance of $3$ m from each other. The currents flowing through first and second wire is $3$A and $4.5$A respectively in opposite directions. The resultant magnetic field at mid point of both the wires is ($\mu_0$ = permeability of free space)

solution.text:
Distance between the wires, $d = 3$ m

Distance of the midpoint from each wire, $r = \dfrac{d}{2} = 1.5$ m

Currents in the wires are $I_1 = 3$ A and $I_2 = 4.5$ A.

Since the currents are flowing in opposite directions, the magnetic fields produced by both wires at the midpoint will be in the same direction.

Resultant magnetic field at the midpoint is given by $B = B_1 + B_2$

$B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I_1}{2\pi r} + \dfrac{\mu_0 I_2}{2\pi r}$

$B = \dfrac{\mu_0}{2\pi (1.5)} (3 + 4.5)$

$B = \dfrac{\mu_0}{3\pi} (7.5)$

$B = \dfrac{2.5\mu_0}{\pi} = \dfrac{5\mu_0}{2\pi}$

Answer: $\dfrac{5\mu_0}{2\pi}$

question.text:
Choose the WRONG Statement from the following statements.
(A) A toroid is a solenoid bent in the form of a closed ring.
(B) The magnetic field lines of solenoid are straight lines parallel to the axis inside the solenoid.
(C) The magnetic field lines of toroid are circular having common centre.
(D) Inside a solenoid, magnetic field may be made strong by passing small current and using laminated coil of soft iron.

solution.text:
Statement (A) is correct because a toroid is essentially a hollow circular ring on which a large number of turns of a wire are closely wound, which is equivalent to a solenoid bent into a closed ring.

Statement (B) is correct because inside a long solenoid, the magnetic field is uniform, meaning the field lines are straight and parallel to the axis.

Statement (C) is correct because the magnetic field lines inside a toroid form closed circular loops with a common centre.

Statement (D) is incorrect because the magnetic field inside a solenoid is given by $B = \mu n I$. To produce a strong magnetic field, a large current $I$ must be passed through it, not a small current.

Answer: D

question.text: Two long straight parallel wires are separated by a distance of $20$ cm. Each wire carries current $5$ mA in the same direction. The magnetic field at a point P midway between them is $\{\mu_0=$ permeability of free space$\}$

solution.text:
The magnetic field produced by a long straight wire carrying current $I$ at a distance $r$ is given by $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}$.

Let the two wires be wire 1 and wire 2. The point P is midway between the two wires, so the distance from each wire to point P is $r = 10$ cm.

The magnetic field at P due to wire 1 is $B_1 = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}$.

The magnetic field at P due to wire 2 is $B_2 = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}$.

Since the currents in both wires are in the same direction, the magnetic field vectors produced by them at the midpoint P will be equal in magnitude but opposite in direction (according to the right-hand thumb rule).

Therefore, the net magnetic field at the midpoint P is $B_{net} = B_1 - B_2 = 0$.

Answer: zero.

question.text: A circular arc of wire of radius of curvature $r$ subtends an angle of $\dfrac{\pi}{5}$ radian at its centre. If current $i$ is flowing in it then the magnetic induction at its centre is ($\mu_0$ = permeability of free space)

solution.text:
The magnetic field at the centre of a circular arc subtending an angle $\theta$ at the centre is given by

$B = \dfrac{\mu_0 i}{4 \pi r} \theta$

Given that the angle subtended by the arc is $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{5}$ radian.

Substituting the value of $\theta$ in the formula, we get

$B = \dfrac{\mu_0 i}{4 \pi r} \times \dfrac{\pi}{5}$

$B = \dfrac{\mu_0 i}{20 r}$

Answer: $\dfrac{\mu_0 i}{20r}$

question.text: A solenoid of 1000 turns is wound uniformly on a glass tube 4 m long and $0.3$ m in diameter. The magnetic intensity at the centre of the solenoid when a current of 4 A flows through it is

solution.text:
Given $N = 1000$, $L = 4\ \text{m}$, $I = 4\ \text{A}$.

The number of turns per unit length is $n = \dfrac{N}{L} = \dfrac{1000}{4} = 250\ \text{m}^{-1}$.

The magnetic intensity $H$ at the centre of a long solenoid is given by $H = nI$.

Substituting the given values:

$H = 250 \times 4 = 1000\ \text{A/m} = 10^{3}\ \text{A/m}$.

Answer: $10^{+3}\ \text{A/m}$

question.text: A square loop ABCD of side L carrying a current $I_1$ is placed at a distance $(L/3)$ from a conductor coplaner with a straight conductor XY carrying current $I_2$ as shown in figure. The net force on the loop will be ($\mu_0$ = magnetic permeability)

solution.text:
The magnetic field produced by the straight wire XY at a distance $r$ is given by $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I_2}{2\pi r}$, directed into the plane of the paper.

The force on the side AB of the square loop, which is at a distance $r = \dfrac{L}{3}$ and carries current $I_1$ in the same direction as $I_2$, is attractive:

$F_{AB} = I_1 L B_{AB} = I_1 L \left( \dfrac{\mu_0 I_2}{2\pi (L/3)} \right) = \dfrac{3\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{2\pi}$

The force on the side CD, which is at a distance $r = \dfrac{L}{3} + L = \dfrac{4L}{3}$ and carries current $I_1$ in the opposite direction to $I_2$, is repulsive:

$F_{CD} = I_1 L B_{CD} = I_1 L \left( \dfrac{\mu_0 I_2}{2\pi (4L/3)} \right) = \dfrac{3\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{8\pi}$

The forces on the sides BC and DA are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, so they cancel each other out.

The net force on the square loop is the difference between $F_{AB}$ and $F_{CD}$ (directed towards the straight wire):

$F_{net} = F_{AB} - F_{CD} = \dfrac{3\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{2\pi} - \dfrac{3\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{8\pi}$

$F_{net} = \dfrac{12\mu_0 I_1 I_2 - 3\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{8\pi} = \dfrac{9\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{8\pi}$

Answer: $\dfrac{9\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{8\pi}$

question.text: A long solenoid carrying a current produces a magnetic field '$B$' along its axis. If the currunt is tripled and the number of turns per cm is halved then new value of magnetic field will be

solution.text:
The magnetic field produced by a long solenoid along its axis is given by $B = \mu_0 n I$, where $n$ is the number of turns per unit length and $I$ is the current.

Given that the new current is $I' = 3I$ and the new number of turns per unit length is $n' = \dfrac{n}{2}$.

The new magnetic field $B'$ is:

$B' = \mu_0 n' I'$

$B' = \mu_0 \left(\dfrac{n}{2}\right) (3I)$

$B' = \dfrac{3}{2} \mu_0 n I$

$B' = \dfrac{3}{2} B$

Answer: $\dfrac{3}{2}B$

question.text:
The magnetic induction produced inside an ideal solenoid, depends on which of the following quantities ?
(a) number of turns per unit length.
(b) radius of the wire.
(c) current flowing throught it.
(d) permeability of the medium.

solution.text:
The magnetic induction inside an ideal solenoid is given by the formula $B = \mu n I$.

Here, $\mu$ is the permeability of the medium inside the solenoid, $n$ is the number of turns per unit length, and $I$ is the current flowing through the solenoid.

The magnetic induction does not depend on the radius of the wire or the radius of the solenoid.

Thus, it depends on the number of turns per unit length, the current flowing through it, and the permeability of the medium.

Answer: (a), (c) and (d)

question.text: A straight long wire is carrying current I. The ratio of magnetic field due to this wire at perpendicular distance 2 cm and 5 cm respectively from the wire is

solution.text:
The magnetic field due to a long straight wire carrying current $I$ at a perpendicular distance $r$ is given by $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2 \pi r}$.

This implies that $B \propto \dfrac{1}{r}$.

Given $r_1 = 2\text{ cm}$ and $r_2 = 5\text{ cm}$.

The ratio of the magnetic fields is $\dfrac{B_1}{B_2} = \dfrac{r_2}{r_1} = \dfrac{5}{2}$.

Thus, the required ratio is $5:2$.

Answer: $5:2$

question.text: In the following figure, the magnitude of the magnetic field at point 'O' will be

solution.text:
The magnetic field at point $O$ is the vector sum of the magnetic fields produced by the three segments of the current-carrying wire: the semi-infinite straight wire $AB$, the quarter-circular arc $BC$, and the semi-infinite straight wire $CD$.

For the semi-infinite straight wire $AB$, the perpendicular distance from $O$ is $r$. One end of the wire is at $B$ (subtending angle $0^\circ$) and the other extends to infinity (subtending angle $90^\circ$). The magnitude of the magnetic field at $O$ is:
$B_1 = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi r} (\sin 90^\circ + \sin 0^\circ) = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi r}$
By the right-hand rule, the direction of this field is out of the plane of the paper.

For the quarter-circular arc $BC$ of radius $r$, the angle subtended at the center $O$ is $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$. The magnitude of the magnetic field at $O$ is:
$B_2 = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi} \dfrac{(\pi/2)}{r} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi r} \left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$
The current flows from $B$ to $C$ in a counter-clockwise sense relative to $O$. By the right-hand rule, the direction of this field is also out of the plane of the paper.

For the semi-infinite straight wire $CD$, the perpendicular distance from $O$ is $r$. One end is at $C$ (subtending angle $0^\circ$) and the other extends to infinity (subtending angle $90^\circ$). The magnitude of the magnetic field at $O$ is:
$B_3 = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi r} (\sin 90^\circ + \sin 0^\circ) = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi r}$
By the right-hand rule, the direction of this field is out of the plane of the paper.

Since all three magnetic field components are in the same direction, the net magnetic field at $O$ is their sum:
$B_{net} = B_1 + B_2 + B_3$
$B_{net} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi r} + \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi r} \left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) + \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi r}$
$B_{net} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi r} \left(1 + \dfrac{\pi}{2} + 1\right) = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi r} \left(2 + \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$

Answer: $\dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{I}{r}\left(2+\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$

question.text: The ratio of magnetic field at the centre of the current carrying circular loop and its magnetic moment is '$x$'. When both the current and radius are tripled, then the ratio will be

solution.text:
Magnetic field at the centre of a circular loop is $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2R}$

Magnetic moment of the loop is $M = I \pi R^2$

The ratio is $x = \dfrac{B}{M} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2R \cdot I \pi R^2} = \dfrac{\mu_0}{2 \pi R^3}$

When current and radius are tripled, $I' = 3I$ and $R' = 3R$

New magnetic field $B' = \dfrac{\mu_0 (3I)}{2(3R)} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2R} = B$

New magnetic moment $M' = (3I) \pi (3R)^2 = 27 I \pi R^2 = 27 M$

New ratio $x' = \dfrac{B'}{M'} = \dfrac{B}{27M} = \dfrac{x}{27}$

Answer: $\dfrac{x}{27}$

question.text: The magnetic field at the center of circular coil carrying current '$I$' for a single turn of a given length of wire is '$B$'. The same wire is bent in a circular coil having two turns. When the same current passes through it, the value of magnetic field becomes

solution.text:
Let the length of the wire be $L$.

For a single turn coil, the radius $R_1$ is given by $2\pi R_1 = L \Rightarrow R_1 = \dfrac{L}{2\pi}$.

The magnetic field at the center of the single turn coil is $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2 R_1}$.

When the same wire is bent into a coil of $N=2$ turns, the new radius $R_2$ is given by $2 \times 2\pi R_2 = L \Rightarrow R_2 = \dfrac{L}{4\pi} = \dfrac{R_1}{2}$.

The magnetic field at the center of the two-turn coil is $B' = \dfrac{\mu_0 N I}{2 R_2}$.

Substituting $N = 2$ and $R_2 = \dfrac{R_1}{2}$, we get $B' = \dfrac{\mu_0 (2) I}{2 \left(\dfrac{R_1}{2}\right)} = 4 \left(\dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2 R_1}\right) = 4B$.

Answer: $4B$

question.text: The magnetic field at perpendicular distance '$r$' from a long wire carrying current '$I$' is '$B$'. The magnetic field at perpendicular distance '$2r$' from the same wire is

solution.text:
The magnetic field produced by a long straight wire carrying current $I$ at a perpendicular distance $r$ is given by:

$B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}$

This relation shows that the magnetic field is inversely proportional to the perpendicular distance from the wire:

$B \propto \dfrac{1}{r}$

Let the magnetic field at distance $r_1 = r$ be $B_1 = B$.

Let the magnetic field at distance $r_2 = 2r$ be $B_2$.

Taking the ratio of the magnetic fields:

$\dfrac{B_2}{B_1} = \dfrac{r_1}{r_2}$

$\dfrac{B_2}{B} = \dfrac{r}{2r}$

$\dfrac{B_2}{B} = \dfrac{1}{2}$

$B_2 = \dfrac{B}{2}$

question.text: The magnetic field intensity (H) at the centre of a long solenoid having 'n' turns per unit length and carrying a current I, when no material is kept in it is ($\mu_0$ = permeability of free space)

solution.text:
The magnetic field $B$ at the centre of a long solenoid is given by $B = \mu_0 n I$, where $n$ is the number of turns per unit length and $I$ is the current.

The magnetic field intensity $H$ is related to the magnetic field $B$ in free space by the relation $H = \dfrac{B}{\mu_0}$.

Substituting the value of $B$, we get $H = \dfrac{\mu_0 n I}{\mu_0} = nI$.

Answer: $nI$

question.text: A long wire is bent into a circular coil of one turn and then into a circular coil of smaller radius having n turns. If the same current is passed in both the cases, the ratio of magnetic field produced at the centre for one turn to that of n turns is

solution.text:
Let the length of the wire be $L$.

For a circular coil of one turn, the radius $R_1$ is given by $L = 2 \pi R_1 \Rightarrow R_1 = \dfrac{L}{2 \pi}$.

The magnetic field at the centre of the coil of one turn is $B_1 = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2 R_1}$.

For a circular coil of $n$ turns, the radius $R_n$ is given by $L = n(2 \pi R_n) \Rightarrow R_n = \dfrac{L}{2 \pi n} = \dfrac{R_1}{n}$.

The magnetic field at the centre of the coil of $n$ turns is $B_n = \dfrac{\mu_0 n I}{2 R_n}$.

Substituting $R_n = \dfrac{R_1}{n}$, we get $B_n = \dfrac{\mu_0 n I}{2 \left(\dfrac{R_1}{n}\right)} = n^2 \left(\dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2 R_1}\right) = n^2 B_1$.

The ratio of the magnetic field for one turn to that of $n$ turns is $\dfrac{B_1}{B_n} = \dfrac{1}{n^2}$.

Answer: $1 : n^2$

question.text:
A thin ring of radius 'R' metre has charge 'q' coulomb uniformly spread on it. The ring rotates about its axis with a constant frequency of 'f' revolution/s. The value of magnetic induction at the centre of the ring in $\text{Wb/m}^2$ is

( $\mu_0$ = permeability of free space )

solution.text:
The equivalent current $I$ due to the rotating charge is given by the rate of flow of charge.

$I = \dfrac{q}{T} = qf$

The magnetic induction at the centre of a circular current-carrying loop is given by:

$B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2R}$

Substituting the value of $I$, we get:

$B = \dfrac{\mu_0 qf}{2R}$

Answer: $\dfrac{\mu_0 qf}{2R}$

question.text:
A rod with a circular cross-section area $2$ cm$^2$ and length $40$ cm is wound uniformly with $400$ turns of an insulated wire. If a current $0.4$ A flows in the wire winding, the total magnetic flux produced inside the winding is $4\pi \times 10^{-6}$ Wb. The relative permeability of the rod is
(Given permeability of vacuum $\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}$ N m A$^{-2}$)

solution.text:
The magnetic flux $\Phi$ inside the solenoid is given by $\Phi = B A$, where $B$ is the magnetic field and $A$ is the cross-sectional area.

Substituting the given values, the magnetic field is:

$B = \dfrac{\Phi}{A} = \dfrac{4\pi \times 10^{-6}}{2 \times 10^{-4}} = 2\pi \times 10^{-2} \text{ T}$

The magnetic field inside a solenoid with a core of relative permeability $\mu_r$ is also given by:

$B = \mu_0 \mu_r n I = \mu_0 \mu_r \dfrac{N}{l} I$

Substituting the known values into the equation:

$2\pi \times 10^{-2} = 4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times \mu_r \times \dfrac{400}{0.4} \times 0.4$

$2\pi \times 10^{-2} = 4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times \mu_r \times 400$

$2\pi \times 10^{-2} = 16\pi \times 10^{-5} \times \mu_r$

Solving for $\mu_r$:

$\mu_r = \dfrac{2\pi \times 10^{-2}}{16\pi \times 10^{-5}} = \dfrac{1000}{8} = 125$

Answer: $125$

question.text: The magnetic flux near the axis and inside the air core solenoid of length 60 cm carrying current I is $\dfrac{\pi}{2} \times 10^{-6}$ Wb. Its magnetic moment will be (cross-sectional area is very small as compared to length of solenoid, $\mu_0$ = Permeability of free space = $4\pi \times 10^{-7}$ SI unit)

solution.text:
The magnetic field inside a long solenoid is given by $B = \mu_0 n I = \mu_0 \dfrac{N}{L} I$.

The magnetic flux through the cross-section of the solenoid is $\Phi = B A = \mu_0 \dfrac{N I A}{L}$.

The magnetic moment of the solenoid is $M = N I A$.

Substituting $M$ into the flux equation, we get $\Phi = \dfrac{\mu_0 M}{L}$.

Rearranging for $M$, we have $M = \dfrac{\Phi L}{\mu_0}$.

Given $\Phi = \dfrac{\pi}{2} \times 10^{-6} \text{ Wb}$, $L = 60 \text{ cm} = 0.6 \text{ m}$, and $\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7} \text{ T m/A}$.

$M = \dfrac{\dfrac{\pi}{2} \times 10^{-6} \times 0.6}{4\pi \times 10^{-7}}$

$M = \dfrac{0.3\pi \times 10^{-6}}{4\pi \times 10^{-7}}$

$M = \dfrac{0.3}{4} \times 10 = \dfrac{3}{4} = 0.75 \text{ Am}^2$

Answer: $0.75 \text{ Am}^2$

question.text: Two parallel wires of equal lengths are separated by a distance of $3$ m from each other. The currents flowing through first and second wire is $3$ A and $4.5$ A respectively in opposite directions. The resultant magnetic field at mid point of both the wires is ($\mu_0$=permeability of free space)

solution.text:
Distance between the wires, $d = 3$ m.

Distance of the midpoint from each wire, $r = \dfrac{d}{2} = 1.5$ m.

Current in the first wire, $I_1 = 3$ A.

Current in the second wire, $I_2 = 4.5$ A.

Since the currents are flowing in opposite directions, the magnetic fields produced by both wires at the midpoint will be in the same direction.

The resultant magnetic field at the midpoint is $B = B_1 + B_2$.

$B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I_1}{2\pi r} + \dfrac{\mu_0 I_2}{2\pi r}$

$B = \dfrac{\mu_0}{2\pi r} (I_1 + I_2)$

Substituting the given values:

$B = \dfrac{\mu_0}{2\pi (1.5)} (3 + 4.5)$

$B = \dfrac{\mu_0}{2\pi (1.5)} (7.5)$

$B = \dfrac{5\mu_0}{2\pi}$

Answer: $\dfrac{5\mu_0}{2\pi}$

question.text: Two long parallel wires carrying currents $8$A and $15$A in opposite directions are placed at a distance of $7$ cm from each other. A point P is at equidistant from both the wires such that the lines joining the point P to the wires are perpendicular to each other. The magnetic field at P is ___ $\times 10^{-6}$ T. (Given: $\sqrt{2} = 1.4$, $\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}$ SI unit)

solution.text:
Let the distance of point P from each wire be $r$. Since the lines joining P to the wires are perpendicular, they form a right-angled isosceles triangle with the distance between the wires as the hypotenuse.

$r^2 + r^2 = d^2 \Rightarrow 2r^2 = (7 \times 10^{-2})^2 \Rightarrow r = \dfrac{7}{\sqrt{2}} \times 10^{-2}$ m

The magnetic fields due to the two wires at point P are:

$B_1 = \dfrac{\mu_0 I_1}{2\pi r}$ and $B_2 = \dfrac{\mu_0 I_2}{2\pi r}$

Since the position vectors from the wires to point P are perpendicular to each other, the magnetic field vectors $\vec{B}_1$ and $\vec{B}_2$ are also perpendicular to each other.

The net magnetic field at P is:

$B = \sqrt{B_1^2 + B_2^2} = \dfrac{\mu_0}{2\pi r} \sqrt{I_1^2 + I_2^2}$

Substituting the given values:

$B = \dfrac{2 \times 10^{-7}}{\dfrac{7}{\sqrt{2}} \times 10^{-2}} \sqrt{8^2 + 15^2}$

$B = \dfrac{2 \sqrt{2} \times 10^{-5}}{7} \times 17$

$B = \dfrac{34 \times 1.4}{7} \times 10^{-5}$

$B = 34 \times 0.2 \times 10^{-5} = 6.8 \times 10^{-5} \text{ T} = 68 \times 10^{-6} \text{ T}$

Answer: $68$

question.text: A circular coil carrying current has radius ' $R$ '. The distance from the centre of the coil on the axis where the magnetic induction will be $\frac{1}{27}$ th to its value at the centre of the coil is

solution.text:
The magnetic induction at the centre of a circular coil of radius $R$ is given by

$B_{c} = \dfrac{\mu_{0} I}{2R}$

The magnetic induction at a distance $x$ on the axis of the coil is given by

$B_{a} = \dfrac{\mu_{0} I R^{2}}{2(R^{2} + x^{2})^{3/2}}$

Given that $B_{a} = \dfrac{1}{27} B_{c}$, we have

$\dfrac{\mu_{0} I R^{2}}{2(R^{2} + x^{2})^{3/2}} = \dfrac{1}{27} \left( \dfrac{\mu_{0} I}{2R} \right)$

$\dfrac{R^{2}}{(R^{2} + x^{2})^{3/2}} = \dfrac{1}{27 R}$

$\dfrac{R^{3}}{(R^{2} + x^{2})^{3/2}} = \dfrac{1}{27}$

Taking the cube root on both sides, we get

$\dfrac{R}{\sqrt{R^{2} + x^{2}}} = \dfrac{1}{3}$

Squaring both sides, we get

$\dfrac{R^{2}}{R^{2} + x^{2}} = \dfrac{1}{9}$

$9R^{2} = R^{2} + x^{2}$

$x^{2} = 8R^{2}$

$x = 2\sqrt{2}R$

Answer: $2 \sqrt{2} \mathrm{R}$

question.text: A current carrying circular coil of radius ' R ' produces magnetic fields ' $\mathrm{B}_1$ ' and ' $\mathrm{B}_2$ ' at an axial point ' P ' at a distance ' x ' from its centre and at a point ' $Q$ ' placed at its centre respectively. If $B_1=\frac{B_2}{8}$, the value of ' $x$ ' is

solution.text:
The magnetic field at the centre of a circular coil of radius $R$ is given by

$B_2 = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2 R}$

The magnetic field at an axial point at a distance $x$ from the centre is given by

$B_1 = \dfrac{\mu_0 I R^2}{2 (R^2 + x^2)^{3/2}}$

Given that $B_1 = \dfrac{B_2}{8}$, we have

$\dfrac{\mu_0 I R^2}{2 (R^2 + x^2)^{3/2}} = \dfrac{1}{8} \left( \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2 R} \right)$

$\dfrac{R^2}{(R^2 + x^2)^{3/2}} = \dfrac{1}{8 R}$

$(R^2 + x^2)^{3/2} = 8 R^3$

Taking the cube root on both sides, we get

$(R^2 + x^2)^{1/2} = 2 R$

Squaring both sides, we get

$R^2 + x^2 = 4 R^2$

$x^2 = 3 R^2$

$x = R \sqrt{3}$

Answer: $\mathrm{R} \sqrt{3}$

question.text: Two long straight parallel conductors carry currents ' $\mathrm{I}_1{ }^{\prime}$ and ' $\mathrm{I}_2{ }^{\prime}$ $\left(\mathrm{I}_1>\mathrm{I}_2\right)$. When direction of ' $\mathrm{I}_1$ ' and ' $\mathrm{I}_2$ ' is same, the magnetic field intensity midway between two conductors is $20 \mu \mathrm{~T}$. If direction of ' $\mathrm{I}_2$ ' is reversed, the field intensity becomes $50 \mu \mathrm{~T}$. The ratio $\mathrm{I}_2 / \mathrm{I}_1$ is

solution.text:
Let the distance between the two conductors be $2r$. The magnetic field at the midpoint due to a current $I$ is $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}$.

When the currents are in the same direction, the magnetic fields at the midpoint are in opposite directions. Since $I_1 > I_2$, the net magnetic field is:

$B_1 = \dfrac{\mu_0}{2\pi r}(I_1 - I_2) = 20 \mu\text{T}$

When the direction of $I_2$ is reversed, the currents are in opposite directions, so the magnetic fields at the midpoint are in the same direction. The net magnetic field is:

$B_2 = \dfrac{\mu_0}{2\pi r}(I_1 + I_2) = 50 \mu\text{T}$

Dividing the two equations, we get:

$\dfrac{I_1 - I_2}{I_1 + I_2} = \dfrac{20}{50} = \dfrac{2}{5}$

$5I_1 - 5I_2 = 2I_1 + 2I_2$

$3I_1 = 7I_2$

$\dfrac{I_2}{I_1} = \dfrac{3}{7}$

Answer: $\frac{3}{7}$

question.text: An infinitely long straight conductor carrying current ' $I$ ' is bent into a shape as shown in figure. The radius of the circular loop is ' $r$ '. The magnetic induction at the centre of the loop at point ' $o$ ' is $\text { ( } \mu_0=\text { permeability of free space) }$

solution.text:
The given conductor can be considered as a combination of an infinitely long straight wire and a circular loop of radius $r$.

1. Magnetic field due to the infinitely long straight wire at the center 'o':
The straight wire is at a perpendicular distance $r$ from the center 'o'.
Magnitude: $B_{straight} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}$
Direction: According to the right-hand thumb rule, since the current is flowing towards the right and point 'o' is above the wire, the magnetic field at 'o' is directed outwards (perpendicular to the plane of the paper, $\odot$).

2. Magnetic field due to the circular loop at its center 'o':
Magnitude: $B_{loop} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2r}$
Direction: The current in the circular loop is flowing in a clockwise direction. According to the right-hand thumb rule, the magnetic field at the center 'o' is directed inwards (perpendicular to the plane of the paper, $\otimes$).

3. Net magnetic field at the center 'o':
Since the magnetic fields due to the straight wire and the circular loop are in opposite directions, the net magnetic induction is the difference of their magnitudes.
$B_{net} = B_{loop} - B_{straight}$
$B_{net} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2r} - \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}$
$B_{net} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}(\pi - 1)$

Answer: $\frac{\mu_0 \mathrm{I}}{2 \pi \mathrm{r}}(\pi-1)$

question.text: A circular coil carrying current 'I' has a radius ' $r$ ' and ' $n$ ' turns. The magnetic field along the axis of a coil at a distance ' $2 \sqrt{2} r$ ' from its centre is ( $\mu_0=$ permeability of free space, $n$ is very small)

solution.text:
The magnetic field along the axis of a circular coil of $n$ turns is given by

$B = \dfrac{\mu_0 n I r^2}{2(r^2 + x^2)^{3/2}}$

Given $x = 2\sqrt{2}r$, we have

$x^2 = (2\sqrt{2}r)^2 = 8r^2$

Substituting this into the formula, we get

$B = \dfrac{\mu_0 n I r^2}{2(r^2 + 8r^2)^{3/2}}$

$B = \dfrac{\mu_0 n I r^2}{2(9r^2)^{3/2}}$

$B = \dfrac{\mu_0 n I r^2}{2(27r^3)}$

$B = \dfrac{\mu_0 n I}{54r}$

Answer: $\frac{\mu_0 \mathrm{nI}}{54 \mathrm{r}}$

question.text: In the following figure magnitude of the magnetic field at the point $p$ is

solution.text:
The given current-carrying wire can be divided into three parts: a vertical semi-infinite straight wire, a semicircular arc, and a horizontal semi-infinite straight wire.

For the vertical semi-infinite wire, the point P lies on its extended axis. Therefore, the magnetic field at P due to this segment is zero, $B_1 = 0$.

For the semicircular arc of radius $r$, the magnetic field at the center is given by $B_2 = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4r}$. According to the right-hand rule, since the current flows in a counter-clockwise direction, the magnetic field $B_2$ is directed outwards, perpendicular to the plane of the paper.

For the horizontal semi-infinite wire, it starts at a perpendicular distance $r$ from point P and extends to infinity. The magnetic field at P due to this segment is $B_3 = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4 \pi r} (\sin 90^{\circ} + \sin 0^{\circ}) = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4 \pi r}$. Using the right-hand rule, the current is directed to the right and P is above the wire, so the magnetic field $B_3$ is also directed outwards, perpendicular to the plane of the paper.

Since both $B_2$ and $B_3$ are in the same direction, the net magnetic field at P is their sum:

$B = B_1 + B_2 + B_3$

$B = 0 + \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4r} + \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4 \pi r}$

$B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4 \pi r} + \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4 r}$

Answer: $\frac{\mu_0 I}{4 \pi r}+\frac{\mu_0 I}{4 r}$

question.text: A long straight wire of radius 'r' carries a steady current 'I'. The current is uniformly distributed over its cross-section. The ratio $\left(\frac{B}{B^1}\right)$ of the magnetic field ' $B$ ' and ' $B^1$ ' it radial distances $\frac{r}{2}$ ' and ' $3 r$ ' respectively, from the axis of the wire is

solution.text:
Using Ampere's law, the magnetic field inside a solid cylindrical wire at a distance $x < r$ from the axis is given by $B_{in} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I x}{2\pi r^2}$.

At $x = \dfrac{r}{2}$, the magnetic field is $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I \left(\dfrac{r}{2}\right)}{2\pi r^2} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi r}$.

The magnetic field outside the wire at a distance $x > r$ from the axis is given by $B_{out} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi x}$.

At $x = 3r$, the magnetic field is $B^1 = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi (3r)} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{6\pi r}$.

The ratio of the magnetic fields is $\dfrac{B}{B^1} = \dfrac{\dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi r}}{\dfrac{\mu_0 I}{6\pi r}} = \dfrac{6}{4} = \dfrac{3}{2}$.

Answer: $\frac{3}{2}$

question.text: The magnetic field intensity H at the centre of a long solenoid having n turns per unit length and carrying a current I, when no material is kept in it is ( $\mu_0=$ permeability of free space)

solution.text:
The magnetic induction $B$ at the centre of a long solenoid is given by $B = \mu_0 n I$.

The magnetic field intensity $H$ is related to the magnetic induction $B$ in free space by the relation $H = \dfrac{B}{\mu_0}$.

Substituting the value of $B$, we get $H = \dfrac{\mu_0 n I}{\mu_0} = n I$.

Answer: nI

question.text: Two current carrying identical coils are kept as shown in figure. The magnetic field at centre ' $O$ ' is ( $N$ and $R$ represent the number of turns and radius of each coil respectively, $\mu_0=$ permeability of free space)

solution.text:
The magnetic field at the center of a circular coil of radius $R$, having $N$ turns and carrying current $I$ is given by:

$B = \dfrac{\mu_0 NI}{2R}$

Since both coils are identical and carry the same current, the magnitude of the magnetic field produced by each coil at their common center is the same:

$B_1 = B_2 = \dfrac{\mu_0 NI}{2R}$

From the figure, the two coils are placed perpendicular to each other. Therefore, the magnetic fields produced by them at the center are also perpendicular to each other (i.e., the angle between $\vec{B}_1$ and $\vec{B}_2$ is $90^\circ$).

The resultant magnetic field $B_{net}$ at the center is the vector sum of $\vec{B}_1$ and $\vec{B}_2$:

$B_{net} = \sqrt{B_1^2 + B_2^2}$

Substituting the values of $B_1$ and $B_2$:

$B_{net} = \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\mu_0 NI}{2R}\right)^2 + \left(\dfrac{\mu_0 NI}{2R}\right)^2}$

$B_{net} = \sqrt{2} \left(\dfrac{\mu_0 NI}{2R}\right)$

$B_{net} = \dfrac{\mu_0 NI}{\sqrt{2}R}$

Answer: $\frac{\mu_0 \mathrm{NI}}{\sqrt{2} \mathrm{R}}$

question.text: The wire loop PQRSP formed by joining two semicircular wire of radii $R_1$ and $R_2$ carries a current $I$ as shown. The magnitude of the magnetic field at the centre ' 0 ' is

solution.text:
The magnetic field at the centre O due to the straight wire segments PQ and RS is zero as O lies on their axes.

The magnetic field at O due to the outer semicircular arc of radius $R_1$ is:

$B_1 = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4 R_1}$ (directed into the plane)

The magnetic field at O due to the inner semicircular arc of radius $R_2$ is:

$B_2 = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4 R_2}$ (directed out of the plane)

Since $R_1 > R_2$, we have $B_2 > B_1$. The net magnetic field at O is the difference between their magnitudes:

$B = B_2 - B_1$

$B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4 R_2} - \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4 R_1}$

$B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4} \left[ \dfrac{1}{R_2} - \dfrac{1}{R_1} \right]$

Answer: $\frac{\mu_0 \mathrm{I}}{4}\left[\frac{1}{\mathrm{R}_2}-\frac{1}{\mathrm{R}_1}\right]$

question.text: A circular coil of wire consisting of ' $n$ ' turns each of radius 8 cm carries a current of 0.4 A . The magnitude of the magnetic field at the centre of coil is $3.14 \times 10^{-4} \mathrm{~T}$. The value of ' n ' is [Take $\mu_0=12.56 \times 10^{-7}$ SI unit]

solution.text:
The magnetic field at the centre of a circular coil of $n$ turns is given by:

$B = \dfrac{\mu_0 n I}{2r}$

Rearranging the formula to solve for $n$:

$n = \dfrac{B \times 2r}{\mu_0 I}$

Substituting the given values ($B = 3.14 \times 10^{-4} \text{ T}$, $r = 0.08 \text{ m}$, $\mu_0 = 12.56 \times 10^{-7} \text{ SI unit}$, $I = 0.4 \text{ A}$):

$n = \dfrac{3.14 \times 10^{-4} \times 2 \times 0.08}{12.56 \times 10^{-7} \times 0.4}$

$n = \dfrac{3.14 \times 10^{-4} \times 0.16}{4 \times 3.14 \times 10^{-7} \times 0.4}$

$n = \dfrac{0.16 \times 10^{-4}}{1.6 \times 10^{-7}}$

$n = 0.1 \times 10^3$

$n = 100$

Answer: $100$

question.text: Two long parallel wires carry currents $\mathrm{I}_1$ and $\mathrm{I}_2\left(\mathrm{I}_1>\mathrm{I}_2\right)$. When currents are flowing in the same direction, the magnetic field at a point midway between the wires is $6 \times 10^{-6} \mathrm{~T}$. If the direction of $\mathrm{I}_2$ is reversed the field at midpoint becomes $3 \times 10^{-5} \mathrm{~T}$. The ratio $\mathrm{I}_1: \mathrm{I}_2$ is

solution.text:
Let the distance between the wires be $2r$. The midpoint is at a distance $r$ from both wires.

When the currents flow in the same direction, the magnetic fields at the midpoint are in opposite directions. Since $I_1 > I_2$, the net magnetic field is:

$B_1 = \dfrac{\mu_0}{2\pi r}(I_1 - I_2) = 6 \times 10^{-6} \text{ T}$

When the direction of $I_2$ is reversed, the currents flow in opposite directions, and the magnetic fields at the midpoint are in the same direction. The net magnetic field is:

$B_2 = \dfrac{\mu_0}{2\pi r}(I_1 + I_2) = 3 \times 10^{-5} \text{ T}$

Dividing the second equation by the first equation, we get:

$\dfrac{I_1 + I_2}{I_1 - I_2} = \dfrac{3 \times 10^{-5}}{6 \times 10^{-6}}$

$\dfrac{I_1 + I_2}{I_1 - I_2} = \dfrac{30}{6} = 5$

$I_1 + I_2 = 5I_1 - 5I_2$

$4I_1 = 6I_2$

$\dfrac{I_1}{I_2} = \dfrac{6}{4} = \dfrac{3}{2}$

The ratio $I_1 : I_2$ is $3 : 2$.

Answer: $3: 2$

question.text: A coil having 9 turns carrying current produces magnetic field $\mathrm{B}_1$ at the centre. Now that coil is rewounded into 3 turns carrying same current. Then magnetic field at the centre $B_2$ is

solution.text:
Let the total length of the wire be $L$.

For a coil of $N$ turns and radius $R$, the length of the wire is $L = N(2\pi R)$, which gives $R = \dfrac{L}{2\pi N}$.

The magnetic field at the centre of the coil is given by $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 N I}{2R}$.

Substituting $R$, we get $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 N I}{2 \left( \dfrac{L}{2\pi N} \right)} = \dfrac{\mu_0 \pi I N^2}{L}$.

Since $I$ and $L$ are constant, $B \propto N^2$.

Given $N_1 = 9$ and $N_2 = 3$.

$\dfrac{B_2}{B_1} = \left( \dfrac{N_2}{N_1} \right)^2 = \left( \dfrac{3}{9} \right)^2 = \left( \dfrac{1}{3} \right)^2 = \dfrac{1}{9}$.

Therefore, $B_2 = \dfrac{B_1}{9}$.

Answer: $\frac{\mathrm{B}_1}{9}$

question.text: Two identical long parallel wires carry currents ' $\mathrm{I}_1$ ' and ' $\mathrm{I}_2$ ' such that $\mathrm{I}_1>\mathrm{I}_2$. When the currents are in the same direction, the magnetic field at a point midway between the wires is $8 \times 10^{-6} \mathrm{~T}$. If the direction of $\mathrm{I}_2$ is reversed, the field becomes $3.2 \times 10^{-5} \mathrm{~T}$. The ratio of $\mathrm{I}_2$ to $\mathrm{I}_1$ is

solution.text:
Let the distance between the two wires be $2r$. The distance of the midway point from each wire is $r$.

When the currents are in the same direction, the magnetic fields produced by the two wires at the midway point are in opposite directions. Since $I_1 > I_2$, the net magnetic field is:

$B_1 = \dfrac{\mu_0}{2\pi r}(I_1 - I_2) = 8 \times 10^{-6} \text{ T}$

When the direction of $I_2$ is reversed, the currents are in opposite directions, and the magnetic fields at the midway point are in the same direction. The net magnetic field is:

$B_2 = \dfrac{\mu_0}{2\pi r}(I_1 + I_2) = 3.2 \times 10^{-5} \text{ T} = 32 \times 10^{-6} \text{ T}$

Taking the ratio of $B_2$ to $B_1$:

$\dfrac{B_2}{B_1} = \dfrac{I_1 + I_2}{I_1 - I_2} = \dfrac{32 \times 10^{-6}}{8 \times 10^{-6}} = 4$

$I_1 + I_2 = 4(I_1 - I_2)$

$I_1 + I_2 = 4I_1 - 4I_2$

$5I_2 = 3I_1$

$\dfrac{I_2}{I_1} = \dfrac{3}{5}$

Answer: $3: 5$

question.text: Two very long straight conductors (wires) are set parallel to each other. Each carries a current ' $I$ ' in the same direction and the separation between them is ' 2r '. The intensity of the magnetic field at point ' $P$ ' (as shown in the figure) ($\mu_0=$ permeability of free space) is

solution.text:
The magnetic field at a distance $d$ from a long straight wire carrying current $I$ is given by $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi d}$.

Let the left wire be wire 1 and the right wire be wire 2. Both wires carry current $I$ in the upward direction.

The distance of point P from wire 1 is $d_1 = 2r + r = 3r$.
The magnetic field at P due to wire 1 is $B_1 = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi (3r)} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{6\pi r}$.
By the right-hand grip rule, the direction of $B_1$ is into the plane of the paper.

The distance of point P from wire 2 is $d_2 = r$.
The magnetic field at P due to wire 2 is $B_2 = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}$.
By the right-hand grip rule, the direction of $B_2$ is also into the plane of the paper.

Since both magnetic fields are in the same direction, the net magnetic field at P is the sum of their magnitudes:
$B_{net} = B_1 + B_2$
$B_{net} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{6\pi r} + \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}$
$B_{net} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r} \left( \dfrac{1}{3} + 1 \right)$
$B_{net} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r} \left( \dfrac{4}{3} \right)$
$B_{net} = \dfrac{2}{3} \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{\pi r}$

Answer: $\frac{2}{3} \frac{\mu_0 \mathrm{I}}{\pi \mathrm{r}}$

question.text: A long wire carrying a steady current is bent into a circle of single turn. The magnetic field at the centre of the coil is ' B '. If it is bent into a circular loop of radius ' $\mathrm{r}_1{ }^{\prime}$ having ' n ' turns, the magnetic field at the centre of the coil for same current is

solution.text:
Let the length of the wire be $L$.

For a single turn circular loop of radius $R$, the length is $L = 2\pi R \Rightarrow R = \dfrac{L}{2\pi}$.

The magnetic field at the centre of this coil is $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2R}$.

When the same wire is bent into a circular loop of $n$ turns of radius $r_1$, the length is $L = n(2\pi r_1) \Rightarrow r_1 = \dfrac{L}{2\pi n} = \dfrac{R}{n}$.

The magnetic field at the centre of the new coil is $B' = \dfrac{\mu_0 n I}{2r_1}$.

Substituting $r_1 = \dfrac{R}{n}$, we get $B' = \dfrac{\mu_0 n I}{2\left(\dfrac{R}{n}\right)} = n^2 \left(\dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2R}\right) = n^2 B$.

Answer: $\mathrm{n}^2 \mathrm{~B}$

question.text: A wire has three different sections as shown in figure. The magnitude of the magnetic field produced at the centre ' 0 ' of the semicircle by three sections together is ( $\mu_0=$ permiability of free space)

solution.text:
The magnetic field at point $O$ is the vector sum of the magnetic fields produced by the three sections of the wire.

For the straight sections (i) and (iii), the point $O$ lies along the axis of the wires. The angle between the current element $d\vec{l}$ and the position vector $\vec{r}$ is $0^{\circ}$ or $180^{\circ}$.

Using the Biot-Savart law, $d\vec{B} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi} \dfrac{d\vec{l} \times \hat{r}}{r^2}$, the cross product is zero. Hence, the magnetic field at $O$ due to sections (i) and (iii) is zero ($B_1 = 0$, $B_3 = 0$).

For the semicircular section (ii) of radius $R$, the magnetic field at the center is half of the field due to a complete circular loop.

$B_2 = \dfrac{1}{2} \left( \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2R} \right) = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4R}$

The total magnitude of the magnetic field at $O$ is:

$B = B_1 + B_2 + B_3 = 0 + \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4R} + 0 = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4R}$

Answer: $\frac{\mu_0 \mathrm{I}}{4 \mathrm{R}}$

question.text:
A particle carrying a charge equal to 1000 times the charge on an electron, is rotating one rotation per second in a circular path of radius ' r ' m . If the magnetic field produced at the centre of the path is $x$ times the permeability of vacuum, the radius ' $r$ ' in $m$ is
$\left[\mathrm{e}=1.6 \times 10^{-19} \mathrm{C}\right] \quad\left[\mathrm{x}=2 \times 10^{-16}\right]$

solution.text:
The equivalent current $I$ due to the rotating charge is given by:

$I = qf$

Given $q = 1000e = 1000 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} = 1.6 \times 10^{-16} \text{ C}$ and frequency $f = 1 \text{ Hz}$, we get:

$I = 1.6 \times 10^{-16} \times 1 = 1.6 \times 10^{-16} \text{ A}$

The magnetic field at the centre of the circular path is:

$B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2r}$

We are given that $B = x \mu_0$, where $x = 2 \times 10^{-16}$. Equating the two expressions for $B$:

$x \mu_0 = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2r}$

$2 \times 10^{-16} = \dfrac{1.6 \times 10^{-16}}{2r}$

$4r = 1.6$

$r = 0.4 \text{ m}$

Answer: $0.4$

question.text:
Two long parallel wires carrying currents 4 A and 3 A in opposite directions are placed at a distance of 5 cm from each other. A point $P$ is at equidistance from both the wires such that the line joining the point $P$ to the wires are perpendicular to each other. The magnitude of magnetic field at point $P$ is
( $\mu_0=$ permeability of free space $=4 \pi \times 10^{-7}$ SI unit)

solution.text:
Let the two wires be at points $A$ and $B$. The distance between them is $AB = 5$ cm.

Let the point be $P$. Given $PA = PB = r$ and $\angle APB = 90^\circ$.

Using Pythagoras theorem in $\triangle APB$:

$PA^2 + PB^2 = AB^2$

$r^2 + r^2 = 5^2 \Rightarrow 2r^2 = 25 \Rightarrow r = \dfrac{5}{\sqrt{2}}$ cm $= \dfrac{5}{\sqrt{2}} \times 10^{-2}$ m.

The magnetic field at $P$ due to the first wire is $B_1 = \dfrac{\mu_0 I_1}{2 \pi r}$.

The magnetic field at $P$ due to the second wire is $B_2 = \dfrac{\mu_0 I_2}{2 \pi r}$.

Since the lines $PA$ and $PB$ are perpendicular, the magnetic fields $\vec{B}_1$ and $\vec{B}_2$ are also perpendicular to each other.

The net magnetic field at $P$ is $B = \sqrt{B_1^2 + B_2^2}$.

$B = \dfrac{\mu_0}{2 \pi r} \sqrt{I_1^2 + I_2^2}$

Substituting the given values $I_1 = 4$ A and $I_2 = 3$ A:

$B = \dfrac{4 \pi \times 10^{-7}}{2 \pi \times \dfrac{5}{\sqrt{2}} \times 10^{-2}} \sqrt{4^2 + 3^2}$

$B = \dfrac{2 \times 10^{-7} \times \sqrt{2}}{5 \times 10^{-2}} \times 5$

$B = 2 \sqrt{2} \times 10^{-5}$ T.

Answer: $2 \sqrt{2} \times 10^{-5} \mathrm{~T}$

question.text: A current 'I' flows in anticlockwise direction in a circular arc of a wire having $\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)^{\text {th }}$ of circumference of a circle of radius R. The magnetic field ' $B$ ' at the centre of circle is ( $\mu_0=$ permeability of free space)

solution.text:
The magnetic field at the centre of a circular arc subtending an angle $\theta$ is given by $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi R} \theta$.

For an arc which is $\dfrac{3}{4}$ of the circumference, the angle subtended at the centre is $\theta = \dfrac{3}{4} \times 2\pi = \dfrac{3\pi}{2}$.

Substituting $\theta$ in the formula:

$B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi R} \times \dfrac{3\pi}{2} = \dfrac{3\mu_0 I}{8R}$

Since the current flows in the anticlockwise direction, by the right-hand thumb rule, the direction of the magnetic field at the centre is upward (perpendicular to the plane and pointing outwards).

Therefore, the magnetic field is $\dfrac{3\mu_0 I}{8R}$ in the upward direction.

Answer: $\frac{3 \mu_0 \mathrm{I}}{8 \mathrm{R}}$ in upward direction

question.text: An arc of a circle of radius ' $R$ ' subtends an angle $\frac{\pi}{2}$ at the centre. It carries a current $I$. The magnetic field at the centre will be ( $\mu_0=$ permeability of free space)

solution.text:
The magnetic field at the centre of a circular arc of radius $R$ carrying current $I$ and subtending an angle $\theta$ at the centre is given by:

$B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4 \pi R} \theta$

Given that the angle subtended by the arc is $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$.

Substituting the value of $\theta$ in the formula:

$B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4 \pi R} \times \dfrac{\pi}{2}$

$B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{8 R}$

Answer: $\frac{\mu_0 I}{8 R}$

question.text: Two coils $P$ and $Q$ each of radius $R$ carry currents I and $\sqrt{8} \mathrm{I}$ respectively in same direction. Those coils are lying in perpendicular planes such that they have a common centre. The magnitude of the magnetic field at the common centre of the two coils is ( $\mu_0=$ permeability of free space)

solution.text:
The magnetic field at the centre of a circular coil of radius $R$ carrying current $I$ is $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2R}$.

For coil $P$, the magnetic field at the centre is $B_P = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2R}$.

For coil $Q$, the magnetic field at the centre is $B_Q = \dfrac{\mu_0 (\sqrt{8} I)}{2R} = \sqrt{8} \left(\dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2R}\right)$.

Since the coils are in perpendicular planes, their magnetic fields at the common centre are perpendicular to each other.

The magnitude of the resultant magnetic field is $B = \sqrt{B_P^2 + B_Q^2}$.

$B = \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2R}\right)^2 + \left(\sqrt{8} \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2R}\right)^2}$

$B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2R} \sqrt{1 + 8} = \dfrac{3 \mu_0 I}{2R}$.

Answer: $\frac{3 \mu_0 I}{2 R}$

question.text: The magnetic induction along the axis of a toroidal solenoid is independent of

options.text: number of turns per unit length.

solution.text:
The magnetic induction $B$ along the axis of a toroidal solenoid is given by the expression:

$B = \mu n I$

where $\mu$ is the permeability of the medium inside the toroid, $n$ is the number of turns per unit length, and $I$ is the current passing through the solenoid.

From the above formula, it is evident that the magnetic induction depends on the permeability, the number of turns per unit length, and the current. It is independent of the radius of the toroidal solenoid.

Answer: radius of the toroidal solenoid.

question.text: Two concentric circular coils $A$ and $B$ having radii 20 cm and 10 cm respectively lie in the same plane. The current in coil A is 0.5 A in anticlockwise direction. The current in coil B, so that net magnetic field at the common centre is zero, is

solution.text:
The magnetic field at the centre of a circular coil of radius $R$ carrying current $I$ is given by $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2R}$.

For the net magnetic field at the common centre to be zero, the magnetic fields produced by coils A and B must be equal in magnitude and opposite in direction.

Since the current in coil A is in the anticlockwise direction, its magnetic field at the centre is directed outwards. Therefore, the magnetic field of coil B must be directed inwards, which implies that the current in coil B must be in the clockwise direction.

Equating the magnitudes of the magnetic fields:

$B_A = B_B$

$\dfrac{\mu_0 I_A}{2 R_A} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I_B}{2 R_B}$

$\dfrac{I_A}{R_A} = \dfrac{I_B}{R_B}$

Substituting the given values $I_A = 0.5$ A, $R_A = 20$ cm, and $R_B = 10$ cm:

$\dfrac{0.5}{20} = \dfrac{I_B}{10}$

$I_B = \dfrac{0.5 \times 10}{20} = 0.25$ A

Thus, the current in coil B is $0.25$ A in the clockwise direction.

Answer: 0.25 A in clockwise direction.

question.text: The strength of magnetic field at a perpendicular distance ' $x$ ' near a long straight conductor carrying current ' $I$ ' is ' $B$ '. The magnetic. field at a distance $\frac{\mathrm{X}}{3}$ from straight conductor will be

solution.text:
The magnetic field $B$ due to a long straight conductor carrying current $I$ at a perpendicular distance $x$ is given by

$B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2 \pi x}$

The magnetic field $B'$ at a distance $x' = \dfrac{x}{3}$ is

$B' = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2 \pi \left(\dfrac{x}{3}\right)}$

$B' = 3 \left( \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2 \pi x} \right)$

$B' = 3B$

Answer: 3 B

question.text: A current carrying circular loop of radius ' $R$ ' and current carrying long straight wire are placed in the same plane. The current through circular loop and long straight wire are ' $I_C$ ' and ' $I_w$ ' respectively. The perpendicular distance between centre of the circular loop and wire is ' d '. The magnetic field at the centre of the loop will be zero when separation ' $d$ ' is equal to

solution.text:
The magnetic field at the centre of the circular loop due to its own current $I_C$ is given by

$B_C = \dfrac{\mu_0 I_C}{2R}$

The magnetic field at the centre of the loop due to the long straight wire carrying current $I_w$ at a distance $d$ is given by

$B_w = \dfrac{\mu_0 I_w}{2\pi d}$

For the net magnetic field at the centre of the loop to be zero, the magnitudes of these two magnetic fields must be equal and opposite in direction.

$B_C = B_w$

$\dfrac{\mu_0 I_C}{2R} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I_w}{2\pi d}$

$d = \dfrac{R I_w}{\pi I_C}$

Answer: $\frac{\mathrm{RI}_{\mathrm{w}}}{\pi \mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{C}}}$

question.text: An infinitely long straight conductor is bent into the shape as shown in the figure. It carries a current I ampere and the radius of the circular loop is r metre. Then the magnetic induction B at the centre of the circular part is:

solution.text:
The magnetic field at the centre of the loop is the superposition of the fields due to the straight wire and the circular loop.

Magnetic field at the centre due to the infinitely long straight wire:
$B_1 = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2 \pi r}$
By the right-hand rule, since the current is flowing to the right, this field is directed outwards from the plane of the paper.

Magnetic field at the centre due to the circular loop:
$B_2 = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2 r}$
Since the current in the loop is clockwise, this field is directed inwards into the plane of the paper by the right-hand rule.

Since the two fields are in opposite directions, the net magnetic field is their difference:
$B = B_2 - B_1$
$B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2 r} - \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2 \pi r}$
$B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2 r} \left(1 - \dfrac{1}{\pi}\right)$
$B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2 \pi r} (\pi - 1)$

Multiplying the numerator and denominator by $2$ gives:
$B = \dfrac{\mu_0}{4 \pi} \times \dfrac{2 I}{r} (\pi - 1)$

Answer: \(\frac{\mu_{\mathrm{o}}}{4 \pi} \times \frac{2 \mathrm{I}}{\mathrm{R}}(\pi-1)\)

question.text: The magnitude of magnetic field at point ' $O$ ' in the following figure will be

solution.text:
The total magnetic field at point O is the vector sum of the magnetic fields produced by three segments of the current-carrying wire: the semi-infinite straight wire AB, the quarter-circular arc BC, and the semi-infinite straight wire CD.

For the semi-infinite straight wire AB, the perpendicular distance to O is $r$. The magnetic field at O is given by:
$B_1 = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4 \pi r} (\sin 90^\circ + \sin 0^\circ) = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4 \pi r}$
By the right-hand rule, the direction of $B_1$ is out of the plane of the paper.

For the quarter-circular arc BC of radius $r$, the angle subtended at the center O is $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$. The magnetic field at O is:
$B_2 = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4 \pi r} \theta = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4 \pi r} \left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$
By the right-hand rule, the direction of $B_2$ is also out of the plane of the paper.

For the semi-infinite straight wire CD, the perpendicular distance to O is $r$. The magnetic field at O is:
$B_3 = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4 \pi r} (\sin 90^\circ + \sin 0^\circ) = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4 \pi r}$
By the right-hand rule, the direction of $B_3$ is out of the plane of the paper.

Since all three magnetic field components are in the same direction (out of the page), the net magnetic field at O is the sum of their magnitudes:
$B_{net} = B_1 + B_2 + B_3$

$B_{net} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4 \pi r} + \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4 \pi r} \left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) + \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4 \pi r}$

$B_{net} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4 \pi r} \left(1 + \dfrac{\pi}{2} + 1\right) = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4 \pi r} \left(2 + \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$

Answer: $\dfrac{\mu_0}{4 \pi} \dfrac{\mathrm{I}}{\mathrm{r}}\left(2+\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$

question.text: A circular arc of radius r carrying current ' $I$ ' subtends an angle $\dfrac{\pi}{8}$ at its entre. The radius of a metal wire is uniform. The magnetic induction at the centre of circular arc is ( $\mu_0=$ permeability of free space)

solution.text:
The magnetic field at the centre of a circular arc of radius $r$ carrying current $I$ and subtending an angle $\theta$ at the centre is given by:

$B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4 \pi r} \theta$

Given that the angle subtended by the arc is $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{8}$.

Substituting the value of $\theta$, we get:

$B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4 \pi r} \times \dfrac{\pi}{8}$

$B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{32 r}$

Answer: $\dfrac{\mu_0 I}{32 r}$

question.text: A long solenoid carrying a current produces magnetic field B along its axis. If the number of turns per cm are tripled and the current is made $\left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)^{\mathrm{th}}$ then the new value of magnetic field will be

solution.text:
The magnetic field produced by a long solenoid along its axis is given by $B = \mu_0 n I$, where $n$ is the number of turns per unit length and $I$ is the current.

Given that the new number of turns per unit length is $n' = 3n$ and the new current is $I' = \dfrac{I}{4}$.

The new magnetic field $B'$ is given by:

$B' = \mu_0 n' I'$

$B' = \mu_0 (3n) \left(\dfrac{I}{4}\right)$

$B' = \dfrac{3}{4} \mu_0 n I$

$B' = \dfrac{3B}{4}$

Answer: $\dfrac{3 B}{4}$

question.text: A current carrying circular loop of radius ' $R$ ' and current carrying long straight wire are placed in the same plane. $I_c$ and $I_w$ are the currents through circular loop and long straight wire respectively. The perpendicular distance between centre of the circular loop and wire is ' $d$ '. The magnetic field at the centre of the loop will be zero when separation ' $d$ ' is equal to

solution.text:
The magnetic field at the centre of the circular loop due to its own current is given by:

$B_c = \dfrac{\mu_0 I_c}{2R}$

The magnetic field at the centre of the circular loop due to the long straight wire at a distance $d$ is given by:

$B_w = \dfrac{\mu_0 I_w}{2\pi d}$

For the net magnetic field at the centre of the loop to be zero, the magnitudes of these two magnetic fields must be equal and opposite in direction.

$B_c = B_w$

$\dfrac{\mu_0 I_c}{2R} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I_w}{2\pi d}$

Rearranging the terms to solve for $d$, we get:

$d = \dfrac{R I_w}{\pi I_c}$

Answer: $\dfrac{R I_w}{\pi I_c}$

question.text: The magnetic field intensity inside current carrying solenoid is $\mathrm{H}=2.4 \times 10^3 \mathrm{~A} / \mathrm{m}$. If length and number of turns of a solenoid is 15 cm and 60 turns respectively. The current flowing in the solenoid is

solution.text:
Given $H = 2.4 \times 10^3 \text{ A/m}$, $l = 15 \text{ cm} = 0.15 \text{ m}$, and $N = 60$.

The magnetic field intensity $H$ inside a solenoid is given by $H = nI$, where $n$ is the number of turns per unit length.

$n = \dfrac{N}{l} = \dfrac{60}{0.15} = 400 \text{ turns/m}$

Substituting the values into the formula for $H$:

$2.4 \times 10^3 = 400 \times I$

$I = \dfrac{2400}{400} = 6 \text{ A}$

Answer: 6 A

question.text: The magnetic induction due to an ideal solenoid is independent of

options.text: total number of turns of the wire.

solution.text:
The magnetic induction inside an ideal solenoid is given by $B = \mu_0 n I$, where $n$ is the number of turns per unit length and $I$ is the current.

Since $n = \dfrac{N}{L}$, where $N$ is the total number of turns and $L$ is the length of the solenoid, we have $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 N I}{L}$.

Thus, the magnetic induction depends on the total number of turns, the length of the solenoid, and the current carried by the wire.

It is independent of the radius of the wire.

Answer: radius of the wire.

question.text: A particle carrying a charge equal to 100 times the charge on an electron is rotating one rotation per second in a circular path of radius 0.8 m . The value of magnetic field produced at the centre will be ( $\mu_0=$ permeability of vacuum)

solution.text:
Charge of the particle, $q = 100e = 100 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C} = 1.6 \times 10^{-17} \text{ C}$

Frequency of rotation, $f = 1 \text{ Hz}$

Equivalent current, $I = qf = 1.6 \times 10^{-17} \times 1 = 1.6 \times 10^{-17} \text{ A}$

Magnetic field at the centre of the circular path is given by $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2r}$

Substituting the values, we get:

$B = \dfrac{\mu_0 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-17}}{2 \times 0.8}$

$B = \dfrac{\mu_0 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-17}}{1.6}$

$B = 10^{-17} \mu_0$

Answer: $10^{-17} \mu_0$

question.text: A thin ring of radius ' $R$ ' carries a uniformly distributed charge. The ring rotates at constant speed ' $N$ ' r.p.s. about its axis perpendicular to the plane. If ' $B$ ' is the magnetic field at the centre, the charge on the ring is ( $\mu_0=$ permeability of free space)

solution.text:
Let the total charge on the ring be $q$.

The ring rotates at a constant speed of $N$ revolutions per second. The equivalent current $I$ due to the rotating charge is the charge crossing a point per unit time, which is given by:

$I = qN$

The magnetic field $B$ at the centre of a circular current-carrying loop of radius $R$ is:

$B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2R}$

Substituting $I = qN$ into the expression for the magnetic field:

$B = \dfrac{\mu_0 q N}{2R}$

Rearranging the above equation to solve for the charge $q$:

$q = \dfrac{2 R B}{\mu_0 N}$

Answer: $\dfrac{2 R B}{\mu_0 \mathrm{~N}}$

question.text: A current of 5 A flows through a toroid having a core of mean radius 20 cm . If 4000 turns of the conducting wire are wound on the core, then the magnetic field inside the core of the toroid is [permeability of free space $=4 \pi \times 10^{-7}$ SI units]

solution.text:
The magnetic field inside the core of a toroid is given by the formula:

$B = \dfrac{\mu_0 N I}{2\pi r}$

Current, $I = 5 \text{ A}$
Mean radius, $r = 20 \text{ cm} = 0.2 \text{ m}$
Number of turns, $N = 4000$
Permeability of free space, $\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7} \text{ T}\cdot\text{m/A}$

Substituting the given values into the formula:

$B = \dfrac{4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times 4000 \times 5}{2\pi \times 0.2}$

$B = \dfrac{2 \times 10^{-7} \times 20000}{0.2}$

$B = \dfrac{4 \times 10^{-3}}{0.2}$

$B = 2 \times 10^{-2} \text{ Wb/m}^2$

question.text: Two identical current carrying coils with same centre are placed with their planes perpendicular to each other. If current $I=\sqrt{2} \mathrm{~A}$ and radius of the coil is $\mathrm{R}=1 \mathrm{~m}$, then magnetic field at centre is equal to ( $\mu_0=$ permeability of free space)

solution.text:
Magnetic field at the centre of a circular coil is given by $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2R}$.

Since the two coils are identical and their planes are perpendicular to each other, the magnetic fields produced by them at the centre will also be perpendicular to each other.

Let the magnetic fields be $B_1$ and $B_2$.

$B_1 = B_2 = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2R}$

The net magnetic field at the centre is:

$B_{net} = \sqrt{B_1^2 + B_2^2} = \sqrt{2} B_1$

Substituting the values $I = \sqrt{2}$ and $R = 1$:

$B_{net} = \sqrt{2} \left( \dfrac{\mu_0 \times \sqrt{2}}{2 \times 1} \right)$

$B_{net} = \dfrac{2 \mu_0}{2} = \mu_0$

Answer: $\mu_0$

question.text: The magnetic field at the centre of a current carrying circular coil of area ' $A$ ' is ' $B$ '. The magnetic moment of the coil is ( $\mu_0=$ permeability of free space)

solution.text:
Let the radius of the circular coil be $r$ and the current be $I$.

The area of the coil is $A = \pi r^2$, which gives $r = \dfrac{A^{1/2}}{\pi^{1/2}}$.

The magnetic field at the centre of the circular coil is $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2r}$.

From this, the current is $I = \dfrac{2rB}{\mu_0}$.

The magnetic moment of the coil is $M = IA$.

Substituting the value of $I$, we get $M = \left( \dfrac{2rB}{\mu_0} \right) A$.

Substituting $r = \dfrac{A^{1/2}}{\pi^{1/2}}$, we get $M = \dfrac{2 B A}{\mu_0} \times \dfrac{A^{1/2}}{\pi^{1/2}} = \dfrac{2 B A^{3/2}}{\mu_0 \pi^{1/2}}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{2 B \mathrm{~A}^{3 / 2}}{\mu_0 \pi^{1 / 2}}$

question.text: Magnetic field at the centre of the hydrogen atom due to motion of electron in $\mathrm{n}^{\text {th }}$ orbit is proportional to

solution.text:
The radius of the $\mathrm{n}^{\text {th }}$ Bohr orbit is, $r_n \propto n^2$.

$$
